en: Very skilled or proficient at something
hook: ADEPT: an ADEPT is an ADEPT-ed expert.
story: Adept. Nobody in Kamal's family could fix anything electrical, except his twelve-year-old niece. She repaired the broken ceiling fan, replaced a frayed charger cable, and even brought the old radio back to life using online videos and a tiny screwdriver. Everyone agreed she was adept at repairs: very skilled and proficient. Adept is usually followed by at or in. Do not mix it up with inept, which sounds similar but means clumsy and unskilled. Synonyms: skilled, expert, proficient.

gre.s: Although new to the job, she proved remarkably ____ at calming angry customers, defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues.
gre.clue: defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues

en: Harmful or unfavorable
hook: ADVERSE: like an ADVERSARY, working against you.
story: Adverse. The fishermen of Kuakata had planned to go out to sea on Monday, but the weather office reported adverse conditions: strong winds, rough waves, and a depression forming in the Bay of Bengal. Every boat stayed on the shore. Adverse means harmful or unfavourable. Medicines can have adverse effects. Careful: do not confuse adverse with averse, which means unwilling, as in averse to risk. Conditions are adverse; people are averse. Synonyms: unfavourable, harmful, hostile.

gre.s: The drug trial was halted early because several participants suffered ____ reactions, including severe rashes and dangerously high fevers.
gre.clue: including severe rashes and dangerously high fevers

en: Suitable or proper for the situation (adj.); to take something for one's own use, often without permission (verb)
hook: Two pronunciations: ap-PRO-pree-it means SUITABLE; ap-PRO-pree-ate means to TAKE as your PROPERTY.
story: Appropriate. Rafi spent a month designing a poster for the university festival. A week later, a senior student printed it with his own name at the bottom. He had appropriated Rafi's work: taken it for his own use without permission. That verb is a GRE favourite. As an adjective, appropriate simply means suitable, like appropriate clothes for an interview. Governments also appropriate funds, setting money aside for a particular purpose. Synonyms for the verb: seize, commandeer, usurp.

gre.s: Critics accused the fashion house of choosing to ____ traditional Jamdani motifs for its new collection without ever crediting the weavers who had developed them over centuries.
gre.clue: without ever crediting the weavers

en: A very typical example; an original model
hook: ARCH-TYPE: the ARCH (chief, first) TYPE.
story: Archetype. Every Bengali child knows folk tales about the clever jackal who tricks the crocodile and the tiger. Hundreds of later stories follow the same pattern: a small, smart animal outwitting a bigger, stronger one. The clever jackal is an archetype: a very typical example, an original model from which others are copied. Arche means first or original, and type means model. Robin Hood is the archetype of the noble outlaw. Synonyms: prototype, model, paragon.

gre.s: The scheming stepmother of old folk tales is the ____ from which countless later villains, in novels and films alike, have been copied.
gre.clue: from which countless later villains

en: Able to express ideas clearly and effectively; to express clearly
hook: ARTICULATE: every ARTICLE of speech placed perfectly.
story: Articulate. At the national debate final, Anika faced a famously sharp opponent. When her turn came, she spoke slowly, chose every word precisely, and explained a complicated economic argument so clearly that even the youngest people in the audience understood. The judges called her articulate: able to express ideas clearly and effectively. As a verb, to articulate is to express clearly: she articulated what everyone had been feeling. Its opposite is inarticulate. Synonyms: eloquent, lucid, fluent.

gre.s: Although the witness was only fourteen, her testimony was remarkably ____, laying out the events in clear, precise sentences that impressed even the hostile lawyers.
gre.clue: laying out the events in clear, precise sentences

en: Showing signs of future success; favorable
hook: AUSPICIOUS: AUSPICES were bird signs Romans read for good luck.
story: Auspicious. Mitu's family chose the wedding date carefully. The elders wanted the cool, dry days of winter, and the date also fell on the bride's grandmother's birthday. When the morning arrived bright and sunny, everyone agreed it was an auspicious beginning: showing signs of future success, favourable. The word comes from Roman priests who watched the flight of birds for omens; such a bird watcher was called an auspex. Synonyms: promising, favourable, propitious. Its opposite is ominous.

gre.s: The campaign's opening day was hardly ____: the candidate's car broke down on the way, and a sudden storm emptied the rally ground before she could speak.
gre.clue: the candidate's car broke down on the way

en: Deprived of something valuable; lacking
hook: BEREFT: BEREAVED, left without.
story: Bereft. When river erosion swallowed Rafiq's grandfather's house and land in a single night, the old man was left bereft: deprived of everything valuable he had owned. He sat on the embankment, staring at the water where his home had been. Bereft can describe grief after losing a loved one, or simply lacking something, as in a speech bereft of ideas. It is related to bereaved, which is used for death. Synonyms: deprived, devoid, destitute.

gre.s: Once its last bookshop and cinema had closed, the town seemed ____ of any cultural life, and young people left for the city as soon as they could.
gre.clue: young people left for the city as soon as they could

en: Tending to find fault over trivial things
hook: CAPTIOUS: tries to CAPTURE you in tiny errors.
story: Captious. Imran's new flatmate complained about everything. The rice was cooked a minute too long. The towel was folded the wrong way. A chair was two centimetres out of place. He never praised anything; he only found tiny faults. He was captious: tending to find fault over trivial things. Captious comes from a Latin word meaning to catch, as in capture: a captious person is always trying to catch you out. Synonyms: carping, nitpicking, hypercritical.

gre.s: Reviewers dismissed the critic's essay as merely ____: instead of engaging with the book's central argument, he spent ten pages complaining about misplaced commas.
gre.clue: complaining about misplaced commas

en: Proving something beyond doubt
hook: CONCLUSIVE: brings the argument to a CONCLUSION.
story: Conclusive. For weeks, Lamia's hostel argued about who was stealing milk from the shared fridge. Everyone had a theory, but nobody had proof. Then the warden checked the corridor camera. The footage showed the night guard quietly drinking it at two in the morning. That was conclusive evidence: proof beyond doubt. Conclusive is related to conclude: it brings an argument to an end. Do not confuse it with conducive, which means helpful. Synonyms: decisive, definitive, irrefutable.

gre.s: Although the early studies were suggestive, they were far from ____, and regulators insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective.
gre.clue: insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective

en: To secretly plan to do something harmful; to combine to produce a result
hook: CON-SPIRE: breathing (spire) together in whispers.
story: Conspire. Three clerks in a government office secretly agreed to approve fake building permits in exchange for bribes, sharing the money every month. When one of them confessed, all three were charged with conspiring to commit fraud. To conspire is to secretly plan to do something harmful together. Con means together and spire means breathe, as in respire: conspirators breathe together, whispering. Events can conspire too: rain and traffic conspired to make Sara late. Synonyms: plot, collude, scheme.

gre.s: Prosecutors alleged that the two executives had met secretly to ____ against their own shareholders, hiding huge losses while quietly selling their own stock.
gre.clue: hiding huge losses while quietly selling their own stock

en: To describe or portray precisely; to mark the boundary of
bn: সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে বর্ণনা করা; সীমা নির্ধারণ করা
hook: DE-LINE-ATE: draw the LINES clearly.
story: Delineate. Before a new school was built in the village, Sabbir, a land surveyor, walked the plot with a measuring tape and drove bamboo stakes into the ground, marking exactly where the school's land ended and the farmers' fields began. He had delineated the boundary: marked it precisely. The word also means to describe precisely: a good report delineates each step of a plan. The word line is inside it, so think of drawing clear lines. Synonyms: outline, define, depict.

gre.s: Because the old treaty failed to ____ the border precisely, both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank.
gre.clue: both countries spent decades claiming the same narrow strip of riverbank

en: To free from something that is tangled or complicated
hook: DIS-ENTANGLE: undo the TANGLE.
story: Disentangle. Priya opened her drawer and found her earphones, phone charger, and a necklace knotted together in one hopeless ball. She sat on her bed for twenty minutes, patiently untwisting each strand until all three were free. She had disentangled them: freed them from a tangle. The word is often used for complicated situations too: a lawyer disentangles a messy family property dispute, separating each claim. Dis means undo: to disentangle is to undo a tangle. Synonyms: untangle, extricate, unravel.

gre.s: It took the auditors nearly a year to ____ the company's true finances from a web of shell companies and deliberately misleading accounts.
gre.clue: a web of shell companies and deliberately misleading accounts

en: To strongly urge someone to do something
hook: EX-HORT: like a coach shouting 'HURT now, win later!'
story: Exhort. On the night before the final, the captain of the university football team gathered his exhausted players. 'We have trained for a year,' he said, his voice rising. 'Tomorrow, run until you cannot run anymore. Do it for everyone who believed in us.' He exhorted them: he strongly urged them to act. Exhort is stronger than suggest; it is urging with passion. Preachers exhort their congregations, and coaches exhort their teams. Synonyms: urge, implore, spur.

gre.s: Health workers went from door to door to ____ families to boil their drinking water, warning that the cholera outbreak could otherwise spread rapidly.
gre.clue: warning that the cholera outbreak could otherwise spread rapidly

en: Physical weakness; moral weakness
hook: FRAILTY: being FRAIL.
story: Frailty. Tanvir's grandmother had once carried water pots from the pond twice a day. Now, at ninety, she needed help to stand, and her hands trembled when she held a cup. Her frailty worried the whole family: her physical weakness. Frailty can also mean moral weakness. In Shakespeare, Hamlet cries, 'Frailty, thy name is woman,' blaming weakness of character. Frail and fragile come from the same Latin root, meaning breakable. Synonyms: weakness, infirmity, fragility.

gre.s: Though his ____ was evident to everyone, since he had to be helped up the steps, the ninety-year-old poet recited for an hour in a voice that never wavered.
gre.clue: since he had to be helped up the steps

en: A real or imagined cause for complaint
hook: GRIEVANCE: something that makes you GRIEVE and complain.
story: Grievance. For three months, the cleaners at Mahin's university had not been paid for their overtime. They wrote a formal letter stating their grievance and submitted it to the administration: a real cause for complaint. A grievance can also be imagined. Mahin's roommate nursed a grievance against him for weeks because he had eaten the last biscuit. Grievance is related to grieve and grave: something heavy on your mind. Synonyms: complaint, grudge, objection.

gre.s: Rather than being addressed, the workers' ____ about unpaid overtime was ignored for months, until it finally erupted into a strike that shut down the port.
gre.clue: until it finally erupted into a strike

en: A long, loud, aggressive speech; to lecture at length
hook: HARANGUE: HARASS with a long rant.
story: Harangue. Zayan came home with a lower score than expected on his mock test. His visiting uncle sat him down and spoke without pause for forty-five minutes: about discipline, about wasted money, about how in his day students studied by candlelight. Zayan could not say a single word. It was a harangue: a long, loud, aggressive speech. As a verb, to harangue is to lecture someone at length. Synonyms: tirade, diatribe, rant. Compare a gentle talk, which is the opposite.

gre.s: What was billed as a friendly welcome speech turned into a forty-minute ____, as the chairman berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect.
gre.clue: berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect

en: A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage
hook: PLOY: a PLOT to deceive.
story: Ploy. Farhan wanted to skip a family wedding to watch a football final. So on the morning of the wedding, he suddenly developed a terrible stomach ache, groaning loudly from his bed. His mother was not fooled. She noticed that his phone was fully charged and the television remote was already beside his pillow. It was a ploy: a cunning plan designed to gain an advantage. Shops use ploys too, like fake sales. Synonyms: ruse, trick, gambit, stratagem.

gre.s: Observers dismissed the minister's visit to the flooded villages, made days before the election with a dozen camera crews in tow, as a cynical ____ rather than a sincere act of compassion.
gre.clue: rather than a sincere act of compassion

en: Graceful, calm, self-controlled manner
hook: POISE: perfectly POISED, balanced and calm.
story: Poise. At her first interview at a big bank, Sara's chair wobbled, her pen ran out of ink, and one interviewer asked a deliberately rude question. Sara simply smiled, borrowed a pen, and answered every question calmly and clearly. Later, the interviewer praised her poise: her graceful, calm, self-controlled manner. Poise originally meant balance or weight, like a scale held perfectly level. A poised person stays balanced under pressure. Synonyms: composure, self-possession, grace.

gre.s: Even when hecklers repeatedly interrupted her speech, the young candidate showed remarkable ____, answering each insult calmly and returning to her argument without missing a beat.
gre.clue: answering each insult calmly

en: Self-important, overly formal behavior or speech
hook: POMPOSITY: POMP and show of importance.
story: Pomposity. At the opening of a new community centre, the local official spoke for an hour. He used long, formal words where simple ones would do, reminded everyone of his many titles, and called himself 'this humble servant of the nation' while demanding the best chair. People laughed quietly behind their hands. His pomposity was hard to bear: self-important, overly formal behaviour and speech. Pomp means grand display, as in pomp and ceremony. Synonyms: self-importance, grandiosity, bombast.

gre.s: The ambassador's ____ was legendary: he insisted on being addressed by all three of his honorary titles and once refused to enter a hall through a side door.
gre.clue: insisted on being addressed by all three of his honorary titles

en: A person authorized to act for another; a substitute
hook: PROXY: like a PROXY attendance a friend gives for you in class.
story: Proxy. Rahim's father could not attend the annual meeting of the village cooperative because he was in hospital. So he signed a letter allowing Rahim to vote in his place. Rahim attended as his father's proxy: a person authorized to act for another. Proxy also means a substitute or stand-in: scientists use tree rings as a proxy for past temperatures, and economists use night-time lights as a proxy for growth. Synonyms: deputy, substitute, stand-in.

gre.s: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages, climatologists use the width of tree rings as a ____ for direct temperature records from that period.
gre.clue: Since thermometers did not exist in the Middle Ages

en: To finally agree after refusing; to become less severe
hook: RELENT: finally LET it go.
story: Relent. For a whole week, Joya begged her parents to let her join the university trip to Bandarban. Her father said no, again and again, worried about the hill roads. Then her teacher called and promised to watch over the group personally. Finally her father relented: he agreed after refusing. Relent can also mean to become less severe: by evening, the rain relented. Its adjective is relentless, meaning never stopping or softening. Synonyms: give in, soften, yield.

gre.s: The authorities refused for months to release the detained journalist, but mounting international pressure eventually forced them to ____.
gre.clue: refused for months

en: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; sometimes, language that is impressive but insincere
hook: RHETORIC: a RHETORICAL question doesn't need an answer — it's just for effect.
story: Rhetoric. Before the student union election, two candidates spoke. The first promised 'a golden new dawn' and 'a campus reborn', without one concrete plan. The second quietly listed three repairs she would make to the library. The crowd cheered the first, but Arif called it empty rhetoric: impressive but insincere language. Rhetoric is also the respectable art of persuasive speaking and writing, studied since ancient Greece. A rhetorical question expects no answer. Synonyms: oratory, bombast, grandiloquence.

gre.s: Voters had grown weary of the candidate's ____, noting that years of grand speeches had produced not a single new road or school.
gre.clue: years of grand speeches had produced not a single new road or school

en: Strictness, thoroughness, and accuracy; harsh conditions
hook: RIGOR: RIGID standards.
story: Rigor. In Mitu's thesis lab, the professor accepted nothing on trust. Every experiment had to be repeated three times, every number double-checked, and every claim backed by a reference. Students grumbled, but their papers were never rejected. The lab was famous for its rigor: strictness, thoroughness, and accuracy. Rigor can also mean harsh conditions, like the rigors of a Himalayan winter. The adjective is rigorous. Synonyms: precision, thoroughness, strictness. Its opposite is laxity.

gre.s: The journal is famous for its ____: every submitted paper is checked by three independent reviewers, and every statistical claim must be reproduced before publication.
gre.clue: every statistical claim must be reproduced before publication

en: Thinly scattered; small in number or amount
hook: SPARSE: SPARE, very little.
story: Sparse. Nadia's grandfather was once very proud of his thick hair. But at seventy, it had become sparse: a few thin strands scattered across the top of his head. Sparse means thinly scattered, or small in number or amount. In a desert, vegetation is sparse. In remote char villages, doctors are sparse. Think of something lightly sprinkled across a wide space. Its opposite is dense or abundant. Synonyms: scanty, meagre, scattered.

gre.s: Attendance at the lecture was ____: barely a dozen listeners sat dotted across an auditorium built to hold five hundred.
gre.clue: barely a dozen listeners

en: Resolutely firm and loyal
hook: STEAD-FAST: holding FAST to your place (stead).
story: Steadfast. When Babu's small grocery shop was failing, most of his friends stopped visiting. One old friend, Habib, came every evening anyway. He helped count the stock, lent Babu money without interest, and told everyone to shop there. Three years later the shop was thriving, and Babu still calls Habib his most steadfast friend: resolutely firm and loyal. Stead means place, as in instead: a steadfast person stays fast in their place. Synonyms: loyal, unwavering, constant.

gre.s: Through years of exile and imprisonment, she remained ____ in her commitment to democracy, refusing every offer of freedom that required her to renounce it.
gre.clue: refusing every offer of freedom

en: Not to be trusted; of doubtful quality
hook: GRE trick: SUSPECT as an adjective means questionable.
story: Suspect. A website promised Ishita a full scholarship abroad if she paid a ten-thousand-taka registration fee within twenty-four hours. The site had spelling mistakes, no physical address, and a phone number nobody ever answered. Her professor said the offer was suspect: not to be trusted, of doubtful quality. As an adjective, suspect is stressed on the first syllable and means questionable. Suspect data and suspect motives cannot be relied on. Synonyms: dubious, questionable, fishy.

gre.s: The study's conclusions are ____, since it was funded by the very company whose product it praises and its raw data have never been released.
gre.clue: funded by the very company whose product it praises

en: Too long, slow, or dull; tiresome
hook: TEDIOUS: like TED talking forever.
story: Tedious. Every Monday morning, Rumana's office held a three-hour meeting. The manager read every line of the weekly report aloud, slowly, including numbers everyone had already seen. People yawned, checked their phones, and stared at the clock. The meeting was tedious: too long, slow, and dull. Tedious comes from tedium, meaning boredom. Copying a thousand addresses by hand is a tedious task. Synonyms: boring, monotonous, wearisome. Its opposite is exciting or engaging.

gre.s: Although the documentary covered a fascinating subject, its endless statistics and droning narration made it ____ for most viewers.
gre.clue: endless statistics and droning narration

en: The state of being strong and energetic
hook: VITALITY: VITAL life energy.
story: Vitality. Every morning at six, Shuvo's eighty-year-old grandmother walks two kilometres around the lake in Dhanmondi, tends her rooftop garden, and argues cheerfully with the vegetable sellers. Her grandchildren, still half asleep, cannot keep up with her. She is full of vitality: the state of being strong and energetic. Vit means life, as in vital and vitamin. A city or an economy can also have vitality, meaning liveliness and growth. Synonyms: vigour, energy, vibrancy.

gre.s: Even at eighty, the sculptor retained a remarkable ____, working twelve hours a day and climbing scaffolding that exhausted assistants half her age.
gre.clue: working twelve hours a day

en: Playfully quaint or fanciful; acting on sudden impulses
hook: WHIMSICAL: full of WHIMS.
story: Whimsical. Lamia's art teacher painted the classroom ceiling with flying fish, umbrellas growing like flowers, and a cat riding a rickshaw through the clouds. The students loved it. Her style was whimsical: playfully quaint and fanciful. The word also describes acting on sudden impulses: one day she whimsically cancelled a test and took everyone to see the river. A whim is a sudden, unexplained desire. Synonyms: playful, fanciful, capricious.

gre.s: The architect's otherwise sober design included one ____ touch: a staircase painted to look like a row of giant piano keys.
gre.clue: otherwise sober design

en: To produce or provide; to give way under pressure
hook: YIELD has two meanings: PRODUCE (a crop yields rice) and GIVE WAY (a yield sign).
story: Yield. In a northern village, farmers tried a new variety of rice developed by agricultural scientists. At harvest time, each field yielded nearly twice as much grain as before: it produced more. The amount produced is also called the yield. But yield has a second meaning: to give way under pressure. Drivers yield to an ambulance, letting it pass, and an old bridge may yield under a heavy truck. Synonyms: produce, give way, surrender.

gre.s: Researchers hoped the new irrigation method would ____ larger harvests, but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever.
gre.clue: but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever
